desc:
For every window of k consecutive elements of nums, find its mode: the value that occurs most often inside the window. If several values tie for the highest count, the mode is the smallest of them. Return the array of modes, one per window, from left to right (it has nums.length - k + 1 entries).

For example, nums = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 1] and k = 3 gives [2, 2, 3, 3]: the windows are [1,2,2], [2,2,3], [2,3,3] and [3,3,1].
hints: Recounting every window costs O(n k). When the window slides, only two values change their frequency by one.
Keep a hash map of frequencies for the current window. The remaining difficulty is getting the best (highest count, then smallest value) entry quickly after every change.

Use a min-heap of pairs (-count, value). Whenever a value's count changes push its new pair; when you read the top, discard it if its count no longer matches the map (lazy deletion). Each push is discarded at most once.
editorial: Maintain freq[value] for the window: add the entering element, decrement the leaving element (deleting the key at zero). After every change to a value push (-freq, value) on a heap, so the heap always holds a correct entry for every value currently in the window, plus some stale ones.

The heap order is exactly 'higher count first, then smaller value'. To read the window's mode, pop while the top pair is stale, that is, while freq.get(value) != -count; the first valid top is the answer. Stale entries are removed once each, so there are O(n) pushes and pops overall: O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Alternative designs use a sorted container ordered by (count, value) with the same complexity.
